fullName: Coherent High-Energy X-ray Sector for In Situ Science

status2026.detail:
All four CHEX branches received first light in July 2025. The APS commissioning chart dated 5 October 2026 lists 28-ID-B,C and 28-ID-F at stage 5, Scientific Commissioning and Early Experiments. It lists 28-ID-D,E and 28-ID-G at stage 4, Technical Commissioning. None has reached stage 6, the general user program. All four were at stage 4 in January 2026. The Beamline Directory still lists B/C as "Not Currently Operational" and D/E, F and G as "Under Development", with on-site access.

CHEX was delivered within the APS-U project scope, formally completed in January 2026. The 22 September 2026 insertion-device table lists interim permanent-magnet undulators with 2.8 cm and 3.0 cm periods upstream and downstream. Core-reliability problems delayed the planned 18.5 mm superconducting pair. The APS Strategic Plan 2025–29 schedules it for 2026 to 2027.

The January 2025 proposal call for run 2025-2 offered a Feature Beamlines proposal type for CHEX. An August 2025 update projected first experiments in late 2025 or early 2026 and general-user entry in late run 2026-1 or early run 2026-2. No station had reached stage 6 on the 5 October 2026 chart, so that schedule has slipped.

tagline: At CHEX, coherent high-energy X-rays are used to study material growth inside reactors, with up to four experiments at once.
summary:
At 28-ID, the Coherent High-Energy X-ray sector, or CHEX, scientists study material growth and reactions inside working chambers. Examples include oxide films in vacuum, gallium nitride in gas reactors and battery electrodes during operation. X-rays at mostly 15,000 to 105,000 electron-volts, or 15 to 105 keV, pass through quartz walls, gases and liquids.

Coherent X-rays have a consistent phase relationship, so scattered waves interfere in patterns called speckle. Scientists infer motion of atoms, islands and defects from changes in these patterns. X-rays from two undulators are divided among four branches, one tunable and three fixed-energy. Thin crystals reflect selected energies from a shared beam into the fixed branches. Up to four experiments can run simultaneously across eight experiment positions. In October 2026, CHEX is in commissioning with interim undulators, and first experiments have begun.

whatAPSUEnables.text:
Speckle measurements require coherent X-rays, but the coherent fraction decreases at higher energies. Before the upgrade, about one 25 keV photon in ten thousand was coherent. Gallium nitride growth measurements therefore used a pink beam without a monochromator, passing the whole undulator peak over an energy band about 1% wide, and still required 10-second frames.

The upgraded electron source is about 19 times narrower and 4 times less divergent horizontally. Its emittance, beam size multiplied by angular spread, decreases from 3,113 to 42 pm·rad by design. A predicted coherent flux gain of about 540 times at 20 keV supports faster single-energy speckle measurements. This value assumes an undulator tuned to 20 keV. Measured flux for the interim CHEX undulators is unpublished. Thin crystals divide one beam among fixed-energy experiments, supporting four simultaneous measurements across the sector.
quantitative: At 20 keV, the design coherent flux is 312 × 10¹¹ ph/s in APS-U brightness mode, compared with 0.6 × 10¹¹ ph/s before the upgrade. FDR Table 1.1 quotes a factor of 540 for an undulator optimized for 20 keV.

Design emittance is 42 pm·rad in brightness mode, compared with 3,113 pm·rad before. APS News reported measured values of 45 pm·rad at 50 mA and as low as 28 pm·rad in round mode in 2024, compared with the previous ESRF-EBS record of 134 pm·rad. The round value is per plane, ε_{x} = ε_{y} = 28.7 pm·rad, because coupling shares emittance between planes.

The Gaussian-beam estimate at 25 keV is about 2% coherent fraction for the flat APS-U beam with a 2.07 m permanent-magnet undulator, compared with about 0.01% for the old APS with a 2.4 m device, about 200-fold. At 60 keV, the fractions are about 0.6% and 0.002%, about 300-fold. This estimate uses storage-ring parameters and FDR Table 1.1 with zero energy spread and is only indicative.
Ju and colleagues measured GaN growth by XPCS in 2019 at 25.75 keV. The pink beam had ΔE/E = 1.3%, with 1.4 × 10¹² ph/s in a 4 × 16 µm spot and 10 s frames.

Ju and colleagues estimated in 2017 that APS-U coherent flux at energies used by 12-ID-D would approach the total flux then available. The predicted optimum energy for coherent transmission through 4 mm of fused quartz is about 23 keV.

FDR Table 4.10 predicts 6.8 to 37 × 10¹² ph/s at 15 keV and 4.2 to 11 × 10¹² ph/s at 60 keV at 28-ID-B. Horizontal × vertical FWHM spots range from 0.8 to 9.8 µm × 0.3 to 3.4 µm. These values assume superconducting undulators.

The sector supports four simultaneous experiments across eight positions. The PDR compares this with a single goniometer or instrument at coherent beamlines such as ESRF ID01; the APS feature page also states four simultaneous experiments.

XPCS signal-to-noise scales with coherent intensity per pixel and the square root of frame time. At fixed signal-to-noise, a 100-fold coherent intensity gain gives up to about 10⁴ shorter correlation times. This is an indicative scaling estimate.

techniques.name: Surface and grazing-incidence X-ray photon correlation spectroscopy
techniques.text: Surface X-ray photon correlation spectroscopy, or XPCS, measures motion from changes in speckle scattered by a surface. For a steady process, software calculates the intensity autocorrelation g_{2}, comparing patterns separated by a delay. During growth, two-time correlations compare every pair of frames to resolve changes in the motion itself. Measurements near the anti-Bragg position, halfway between diffraction peaks, are most sensitive to the top atomic layer and track islands and steps during deposition or etching. Contrast decreases when the illuminated volume exceeds coherence lengths, energy spread is too broad or pixels exceed speckle size. Signal-to-noise scales with coherent intensity per pixel and the square root of frame time.

techniques.name: Coherent diffraction imaging, Bragg CDI and Bragg ptychography
techniques.text: Coherent diffraction patterns from a small crystal are used to reconstruct its 3D image computationally, without an imaging lens. Near a Bragg peak, the reconstructed phase measures atomic displacement along the scattering direction and thus strain. Bragg ptychography scans overlapping spots to extend this method to larger samples. High-energy X-rays penetrate operating cells and provide access to multiple reflections. With 55 µm pixels, the coherent region must be no larger than about 20 × R/E µm, where R is detector distance in metres and E is energy in keV. Twofold oversampling requires about half that size. The region is the beam spot or the crystal, whichever is smaller. Sample motion must remain well below a micrometre.

techniques.name: In situ surface X-ray diffraction / crystal-truncation-rod scattering
techniques.text: Surface diffraction measures the top atomic layers of a crystal. The abrupt surface produces faint streaks between Bragg peaks, called crystal truncation rods. Their shapes depend on surface structure. During layer-by-layer growth, anti-Bragg intensity decreases as a layer reaches half coverage and increases as it completes, repeating each atomic layer. At CHEX, rods and nearby diffuse scattering are measured at 15 to 35 keV through chamber walls. Tuning to an element's absorption edge on the tunable branch adds resonant contrast to distinguish metal ions in complex oxides.

techniques.name: High-energy X-ray diffraction
techniques.text: At 28-ID-G, 75 or 105 keV X-rays penetrate centimetres of many materials for measurements of bulk synthesis, crystal growth, corrosion and samples under load. Furnaces, reactors and thick specimens remain in the beam during measurements. Small Bragg angles place many reflections on a flat area detector at once. At these energies, refraction is weak in beryllium. The design specifies nickel lenses for stronger focusing.

techniques.name: X-ray reflection interface microscopy
techniques.text: X-ray reflection interface microscopy forms a real-space image from X-rays reflected by a surface or buried interface. Reflected X-rays are focused by diffraction through the concentric rings of a zone-plate objective behind the sample. Differences in local reflectivity produce contrast from atomic steps and domains. In the design, the objective sits on the diffractometer arm and the camera on the long-distance positioner. This method was proposed alongside Bragg coherent imaging for geochemical interfaces, including minerals reacting with fluids.

techniques.name: Hard X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy with pulsed-laser deposition
techniques.text: Hard X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy, or HAXPES, measures the energies of electrons emitted when X-rays strike a material. These energies identify elements, chemical states and electronic structure. Higher-energy photoelectrons escape from deeper layers, providing information on buried material. At 28-ID-E, a separate twisted monochromator supplies 10 keV for HAXPES alongside pulsed-laser deposition and surface diffraction. Eres and colleagues' 2019 system operated at 4 to 12 keV with a Scienta EW4000 analyser during oxide-heterostructure growth.

scienceCases.title: Correlated island formation during gallium nitride growth
scienceCases.text: During layer-by-layer gallium nitride growth, islands tend to form where islands existed in the preceding layer. Ju and colleagues measured this in 2019 using speckle during metal-organic vapour-phase epitaxy. Two-time correlations compared each pair of frames near the anti-Bragg position, which is sensitive to the surface. They attributed the repeated island positions to adatoms, surface atoms moving between layers, and to the Ehrlich–Schwoebel energy barrier at step edges. The experiment used a pink beam without a monochromator at 25.75 keV with 10-second frames. The growth reactor planned for CHEX hutch F extends this method to greater coherent flux.

scienceCases.title: Oxide-layer rearrangement during film growth
scienceCases.text: Lee and colleagues measured layered Ruddlesden–Popper oxide growth at APS 33-ID-E in 2014. Molecular-beam epitaxy deposits evaporated atoms onto a film in ultra-high vacuum. X-ray scattering during deposition showed that layers exchanged positions, and the researchers used this process to synthesize the first single-crystal La₃Ni₂O₇ films. The oxide-growth station is now at 28-ID-C. Tunable energy adds resonant contrast near absorption edges to distinguish metal ions. The transfer of the earlier system is inferred rather than documented.

scienceCases.title: Oxygen vacancies in deposited oxide films
scienceCases.text: Eres and colleagues combined pulsed-laser deposition, surface diffraction and 4 to 12 keV HAXPES in 2019. Their measurements linked oxygen vacancies to structural changes in La_{2/3}Sr_{1/3}MnO₃ capped with oxygen-deficient SrTiO_{3−δ}. The material changed between perovskite and brownmillerite structures. Such changes matter for poorly conducting layers in thin-film electronics. Station 28-ID-E has a laser-deposition diffractometer and a 10 keV twisted monochromator for photoelectron measurements.

scienceCases.title: Silicon-carbide growth for quantum devices
scienceCases.text: Defects and crystal quality affect silicon carbide used for quantum bits, or qubits. APS identifies silicon-carbide growth during operation as a CHEX research direction. The 2021 CHEX workshops also covered metal-organic chemical vapour deposition, atomic layer deposition and catalysts. These are proposed applications rather than reported CHEX results.

scienceCases.title: Thin-film deposition and etching
scienceCases.text: Chip fabrication includes deposition and etching of films only a few atoms thick. The APS Strategic Plan for 2025 to 2029 proposes surface scattering and speckle measurements at CHEX during these steps. The measurements would track crystallization, defect formation and strain. High-energy X-rays penetrate chamber walls, allowing measurements during processing.

scienceCases.title: Strain and defects in battery particles
scienceCases.text: Ulvestad and colleagues used Bragg coherent diffraction imaging in 2015 to measure moving dislocations inside operating LiNi₀.₅Mn₁.₅O₄ battery nanoparticles. Dislocations are line defects in a crystal. The CHEX design report cites this as a model for 3D measurements during charging. The proposed electrochemistry and catalysis range is 15 to 35 keV, allowing penetration of electrolyte and cell hardware to study solid–solid, liquid–solid and vapour–solid interfaces.

scienceCases.title: Mineral reactions, corrosion and nuclear materials
scienceCases.text: The design report proposes coherent 35 to 60 keV measurements of mineral–fluid reactions in porous rock, corrosion and nuclear materials under load. It estimates corrosion costs at more than 3% of US GDP. Proposed equipment includes an environmental load frame and a combined interface-microscopy and coherent-imaging instrument for nanoscale measurements during reactions.

insertionDevices.name: APS28#11S, upstream interim source
insertionDevices.type: Planar hybrid permanent-magnet undulator, short canted version
insertionDevices.notes: The device has 74 periods, a minimum gap of 8.5 mm, Keff = 2.49 and E1 = 2.98 keV at minimum gap, and 9.0 kW power. Its beam is inferred to follow the outboard path to the tunable branch.

insertionDevices.name: APS30#6S, downstream interim source
insertionDevices.type: Planar hybrid permanent-magnet undulator, short canted version
insertionDevices.notes: The device has 69 periods, a minimum gap of 9.0 mm, Keff = 2.64 and E1 = 2.54 keV at minimum gap, and 9.0 kW power. Its beam is inferred to follow the inboard path to D/E, F and G.

insertionDevices.name: SCU18.5, planned source, not installed as of September 2026
insertionDevices.type: Planar NbTi superconducting undulator pair in a 4.8 m canted cryostat, with the centre canting magnet inside
insertionDevices.notes: At maximum field, Ky = 2.291 and E1 ≈5.1 keV. The upstream and downstream power through the 2 × 1 mm mask is 698 W and 843 W. FDR Chapter 3 lists a 1.2 m magnetic length, an 8 mm magnetic gap and cryocooler operation at 4.2 K. Core reliability problems delayed installation. The APS Strategic Plan 2025–29 schedules installation for 2026–2027.

source.canting: The two insertion devices are separated by a 1 mrad canting angle. The end magnets deflect electrons by 0.5 mrad and the centre magnet by 1 mrad. The upstream source follows the outboard path to the tunable branch; the downstream source follows the inboard path to the fixed-energy branches.
source.frontEnd: The APS-U canted-undulator front end, or CUFE, has a windowless exit with differential pumping. Its limits are 2 × 10 kW and 280 kW/mrad². Beam positions are measured at GRID XBPM1 and XBPM2 in the exit mask. At 25.4–25.6 m, the CHEX mask has a 2 × 1 mm horizontal × vertical aperture per beam, rather than the standard 2 × 2 mm, with the apertures separated by 1 mrad. A tungsten exit collimator at 26.0 m has a 5 × 5 mm opening. An APS-U-design CUFE was installed at 28-ID and tested with beam on the pre-upgrade ring in November 2018. This was FDR Chapter 1 milestone MS-L2-2300, also described in Chapter 3, Section 3-2.2.1.
source.sourceSizeAndDivergence:
The August 2024 APS storage-ring parameters give the electron beam at an insertion-device straight. In round-beam mode, σx = 12.3 µm, σy = 8.26 µm, σx' = 2.34 µrad and σy' = 3.47 µrad, with ε = 28.7 pm per plane. In flat-beam mode at κ = 0.1, σx = 14.5 µm, σy = 3.08 µm, σx' = 2.75 µrad and σy' = 1.29 µrad. FDR Table 1.1 gives brightness-mode values of 14.7 µm, 3.2 µm, 2.8 µrad and 1.3 µrad in the same order.

For a 2.07 m undulator at 25 keV, the calculated single-electron photon contributions are about 1.1 µm and 3.5 µrad, using σr = √(2λL)/4π and σr' = √(λ/2L). The canted sources are about 1.23 m either side of the straight centre. PDR optics calculations assumed a 50 µm FWHM horizontal source.

branches.name: 28-ID-A/B/C, tunable-energy branch
branches.description: The outboard beam from the upstream undulator passes through a horizontal liquid-nitrogen-cooled DCM at 35 m. Shielded transport at 43.5 to 60.6 m crosses G, with a mini-enclosure for transfocator 1 at 50 m. It continues to B, with a shared hexapod at 64.5 m, and C, with oxide MBE at 72 m. A movable white-beam stop at 69.3 m separates these white- and pink-beam-rated hutches. The FDR range is 5 to 60 keV; the 2026 listed range is 6 to 30 keV.

branches.name: Shared inboard canted beam
branches.description: The downstream undulator beam is 1 mrad inboard of the tunable beam and passes through 2 mm graphite. Three thin single-crystal monochromators at 28.3, 38.3 and 40.2 m reflect different harmonics from this shared beam.

branches.name: 28-ID-A/D/E, fixed 15 keV
branches.description: The diamond (111) monochromator at 28.3 m reflects 15 keV about 23.2° outboard. CRL1 is inside A. The branch continues through D, with a Huber hexapod at 35.5 m, and E, with PLD and HAXPES at 43.0 m. A separate twisted monochromator supplies 10 keV for HAXPES.

branches.name: 28-ID-A/F, fixed 25 or 35 keV
branches.description: The diamond (022)/(004) monochromator at 38.3 m reflects 25 or 35 keV about 23° outboard. Hutch F has F/1 at 45.5 m with a Huber hexapod and F/2 at 49.5 m for MOCVD growth.

branches.name: 28-ID-A/G, fixed 75 or 105 keV
branches.description: The Si(022)/(004) monochromator at 40.2 m reflects 75 or 105 keV about 5° inboard. The as-built G hutch spans about 47.5 to 60.7 m. G/1 is at 52 m with a Huber hexapod, and G/2 is at 56 m. Nickel CRLs are planned. The shielded tunable transport crosses the same hutch.

components.name: Upstream interim 2.8 cm hybrid permanent-magnet undulator APS28#11S
components.distanceNote: Position is approximate. FDR Fig. 3.11 places 2.1 m canted HPMU centres at −1229.5 and +1234.5 mm, about 1.23 m from the straight centre. FDR Table 4.4 gives ±1.25 m for the planned SCUs.
components.text: The alternating magnetic field of this 2.07 m undulator deflects 6 GeV electrons from side to side, producing the tunable branch's X-rays. Today it is an interim permanent-magnet undulator with a 28 mm period, the repeat length of its magnet pattern. At its 8.5 mm minimum gap its fundamental, the lowest of its emission peaks, lies near 3 keV; opening the gap raises it, and higher energies come from odd harmonics, overtones at 3, 5, 7… times the fundamental. A superconducting undulator with an 18.5 mm period is planned to replace it in 2026–2027. That this upstream device feeds the tunable branch is inferred from the APS canting convention and the design's heat-load tables.

specs.plannedReplacement: SCU, 18.5 mm period, 1.3 m in FDR Table 4.4; planned for 2026–2027
specs.feeds: Outboard canted beam to the tunable branch; mapping is inferred.

components.name: Canting magnets, 0.5 mrad + 1 mrad + 0.5 mrad
components.distanceNote: Positions are approximate. End magnets are at each end of the roughly 5.4 m straight, with a 1 mrad magnet at its centre, following FDR Section 3-3.3.5.
components.text: Three steering magnets deflect the electron path by 1 milliradian, or mrad, about 0.06°, between the undulators. This creates two independent X-ray directions in one straight section. The beams drift apart by 1 mm for every metre travelled: about 28 mm at the first crystals and 65 mm at station B. A 1 mrad magnet sits between the undulators and 0.5 mrad magnets at either end of the straight; with the planned superconducting pair, the centre magnet will sit inside the shared cryostat.

specs.beam separation: ≈28 mm at 28 m, ≈65 mm at 64.5 m

components.name: Downstream interim 3.0 cm hybrid permanent-magnet undulator APS30#6S
components.distanceNote: Position is approximate; the upstream-undulator note gives the source-position basis.
components.text: The three fixed-energy branches receive radiation from the second interim undulator, 2.07 m long with a 30 mm period. Its fundamental, the lowest of its emission peaks, is set near 5 keV, so its 3rd, 5th and 7th harmonics fall at 15, 25 and 35 keV. The 15th and 21st harmonics fall at 75 and 105 keV. Each thin crystal reflects one selected energy from the shared beam while transmitting the rest. A superconducting undulator with an 18.5 mm period, whose fundamental is 5.1 keV at full field, is planned to replace it.

specs.feeds: Inboard canted beam to D/E, F and G; mapping is inferred.
specs.harmonics used: 3rd/5th/7th at 15/25/35 keV and 15th/21st at 75/105 keV, for a ≈5 keV fundamental with K ≈1.6
specs.planned replacement: SCU, 18.5 mm × 1.3 m, Ky = 2.291 and E1 = 5.1 keV

components.name: Front-end GRID X-ray beam position monitor, XBPM1
components.distanceNote: Position is approximate. FDR Table 3.9 places the CUFE upstream mask, the XBPM1 location, at 19.4 m. It does not specify the 28-ID location.
components.text: Beam direction is measured inside the accelerator tunnel for electron-orbit corrections that stabilize the X-ray beams. The GRID monitor measures fluorescence excited by the beam in metal surfaces at grazing incidence. It must resolve slow drifts to 12 µm horizontally and 10 µm vertically, and faster motion from 0.01 Hz to 1 kHz to 3.7 and 2.4 µm respectively. A second monitor, XBPM2, is built into the exit mask.

components.name: Front-end photon shutter PS2 and safety shutters SS1/SS2
components.distanceNote: Positions are estimated and are not published for 28-ID. Component order follows FDR Fig. 3.4 upstream of the shield wall.
components.text: A photon shutter, PS2, and two safety shutters, SS1 and SS2, block X-rays and stray radiation inside the tunnel before people enter downstream hutches. They belong to the standard canted-undulator front end of the upgraded APS, rated for two beams of up to 10 kW each and 280 kW per square milliradian at their centres. Their exact positions at 28-ID are not published.

specs.CUFE sequence (FDR Fig. 3.4): clearing magnet / LPPS / SRV → BTFM1 → FM2 → lead collimator → FM3 → GRID-XBPM → PS2/IM1 → SS1 & SS2 → wall collimator → FEV → exit mask/XBPM2 → exit collimator → BIV

components.name: Storage-ring ratchet wall with wall collimator
components.distanceNote: The shield spans about 22.1 to 23.6 m, scaled from the 5 m ruler in MEDSI 2025 Fig. 2.
components.text: The ratchet wall surrounds the accelerator tunnel with thick concrete-and-lead shielding. The X-ray beams leave through a collimator, a small opening in a heavy block, and enter the first optics hutch, 28-ID-A. Radiation outside this opening is blocked by the wall. The front end that crosses the wall is windowless, which the 2025 as-built ray trace confirms.

specs.front-end exit: Windowless, as labelled in the 2025 ray trace

components.name: Front-end exit mask with XBPM2, two apertures, 1 mrad apart
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.6 gives 25.6 m for 28-ID. The Table 4.4 footnote instead places the 2 × 1 mm mask at 25.4 m.
components.text: Each undulator beam passes through a small opening in a water-cooled copper mask. Radiation outside these two openings is absorbed. The CHEX requirement is 2 × 1 mm horizontal × vertical openings, compared with the standard 2 × 2 mm. One design table still lists the standard size. Differential pumping separates the ring vacuum without an exit window, preserving coherence. A second beam-position monitor, XBPM2, is built in.

specs.aperturePerBeam_mm: 2 × 1 horizontal × vertical for CHEX; standard CUFE 2 × 2

components.name: Front-end exit collimator, tungsten
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.6 records path length from the straight-section centre.
components.text: Each beam passes through a 5 × 5 mm opening in this tungsten collimator. It stops bremsstrahlung, the very-high-energy gamma rays made when stored electrons strike leftover gas in the ring, from travelling down the beamline with the X-rays. The narrower upgrade openings contain bremsstrahlung even where monochromators shift the X-ray beam only slightly.

components.name: Canted-undulator white-beam slits 28ID-SL-1
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.6 records path length from the straight-section centre.
components.text: The white beam is trimmed before the crystals by water-cooled jaws with tungsten edges. White beam contains the full undulator spectrum and power. The assignment of SL-1 and neighbouring SL-2 to the two 28-ID beams is not stated. In the same design at sector 34, SL-1 trims the inboard beam.

components.name: Canted-undulator white-beam slits 28ID-SL-2
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.6 records path length from the straight-section centre.
components.text: A second set of water-cooled, tungsten-edged jaws trims the other canted beam before the optics. Separate slit pairs provide independent shaping of the two full-spectrum beams.

components.name: 2 mm graphite heat-load filter, inboard beam
components.distanceNote: The FDR does not specify a position. Placement just before the first single-crystal monochromator is a model assumption.
components.text: The shared inboard beam passes through 2 mm of graphite. It absorbs low-energy X-rays that the thin diamond crystals downstream do not reflect but would otherwise absorb as heat. In the design, the heat load on the first 200 µm diamond falls from 68.7 W to 16.4 W, about four-fold, reducing thermal distortion. The design does not give its position; the model places it just ahead of the first crystal.

specs.PDR alternative: Single-crystal diamond filters to reduce wavefront distortion

components.name: Diamond single-crystal side-bounce monochromator for D/E, 28ID-MN-2
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.7 records path length along D/E from the straight-section centre. FDR Table 4.5 also lists the station position.
components.text: A diamond 100 to 200 µm thick reflects 15 keV X-rays about 23° outboard, away from the ring, into D/E. The remaining radiation passes through to the next crystals. At this angle the diamond (111) reflection reflects the undulator's 3rd harmonic, three times its 5 keV fundamental. The design calls for liquid-nitrogen cooling and a symmetric reflection that preserves the beam's collimation. Station E also receives 10 keV from a separate twisted monochromator, whose design is unpublished.

specs.HAXPES beam: Separate 10 keV "twisted" monochromator; design is unpublished

components.name: Secondary collimator 28ID-SC-1, after first SCM
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.6 records path length from the straight-section centre.
components.text: A shielding block confines stray radiation just after the first diamond crystal. Small openings let the two main beams through, while the block stops stray radiation travelling with them from spreading along the beamline.

components.name: Mono-beam slits 28ID-SL-6
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.7 records path length along D/E from the straight-section centre.
components.text: The reflected 15 keV beam is trimmed by adjustable jaws before its first lens stack. Passing only the central part of the beam, with the highest transverse coherence, keeps the speckle contrast high at stations D and E.

components.name: CRL unit 1 for D and E, 28ID-CR-4
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.7 records path length along D/E from the straight-section centre.
components.text: The first D/E focusing stage uses stacked beryllium compound refractive lenses, or CRLs, inside the optics hutch. Refraction is weak in each lens, so many are required. The design allows up to 19 lenses for station D and 10 for station E, each with a 50 µm tip radius. Changing lens counts here and near the sample changes spot size while keeping the focal plane fixed.

components.name: Beam visualization monitor 28ID-BD-3
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.7 records path length along D/E from the straight-section centre.
components.text: Staff align the 15 keV beam using a fluorescent screen and camera. The screen glows where the X-rays strike it, so staff can see the invisible beam while aligning the D/E optics.

components.name: Monochromatic shutter 28ID-SH-2, P8-20
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.7 records path length along D/E from the straight-section centre.
components.text: The D/E shutter blocks the monochromatic, single-energy beam. Closing it makes hutches D and E safe to enter without interrupting the other three branches.

components.name: Beam visualization monitor 28ID-BD-1
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.6 records path length from the straight-section centre.
components.text: Staff align the tunable beam using a fluorescent screen and camera just before its monochromator.

components.name: Shielded pipe through A, 28ID-ST-2
components.distanceNote: The position is not tabulated. The pipe is drawn approximately from SH-2 to the A outboard wall at about 33.4 m path length.
components.text: The 15 keV beam travels through a shielded pipe from the optics hutch's side wall into D. Bent 23° outboard by its diamond crystal, the D/E branch leaves 28-ID-A about 33 m along its path.

components.name: Mono-beam slits 28ID-SL-7
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.7 records path length along D/E from the straight-section centre.
components.text: The 15 keV beam is trimmed just before station D's second lens stack. At each CHEX station, slits, a lens stack and a vacuum window are placed within about 3 m of the sample.

components.name: Collimator 28ID-BC-1
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.6 records path length from the straight-section centre.
components.text: Stray radiation is blocked by a collimator ahead of the tunable branch's monochromator. Its heavy block stops stray radiation travelling with the beam, while a small opening lets the X-rays through.

components.name: CRL unit 2 for D, 28ID-CR-5
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.7 records path length along D/E from the straight-section centre.
components.text: The second focusing stage at D is 1.5 m before the sample, with up to 64 beryllium lenses of 50 µm tip radius. Changing lens counts between this stack and the first one changes the spot at 15 keV from about 1.5 × 0.5 µm to 6.4 × 2.2 µm horizontally × vertically without moving the focus. The design flux at D is 4.4–10 × 10¹² photons per second, calculated for the planned superconducting undulators.

components.name: Window 28ID-WN-3
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.7 records path length along D/E from the straight-section centre.
components.text: The beamline vacuum ends at a thin diamond or beryllium window 1.2 m before station D's sample. These low-atomic-number materials transmit X-rays with little absorption. From here the beam reaches the sample environment.

components.name: Horizontal high-heat-load double-crystal monochromator 28ID-MN-1
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.6 records path length from the straight-section centre. FDR Table 4.5 also lists the station position.
components.text: In the tunable monochromator, two silicon crystals select X-rays according to Bragg's law, matching wavelength to crystal spacing and reflection angle. Rotating them changes the selected energy. Horizontal reflection reduces the effect of vibration on brightness. The outgoing beam is parallel to the incoming beam with a fixed lateral displacement of a few millimetres as energy changes. This is a fixed-exit design. The crystals are cooled with liquid nitrogen. The predicted heat load with the planned superconducting undulator is 697 W. The design gives 5–60 keV, a 2025 paper gives 15–60 keV, and the 2026 directory lists 6–30 keV with Si(111) crystals. A second Si(311) pair and an optional multilayer monochromator are in the design; their as-built status is unknown.

specs.energyRange_keV: 5–60 in FDR; 15–60 in MEDSI 2025; 6–30 in the 2026 directory
specs.position option: DCM or DMM in FDR Fig. 4.3

components.name: 28-ID-D general-purpose Huber hexapod diffractometer
components.distanceNote: The station position is tabulated in FDR Table 4.5.
components.text: Visiting reaction cells are mounted on a Huber hexapod diffractometer. Its six-legged platform and rotation stage set sample angles precisely for battery, catalyst and heated-gas measurements. In the design, the expected spot ranges from about 1.5 × 0.5 µm to 6.4 × 2.2 µm at 15 keV. When the rear hutch E is in use, the instrument retracts in beam-pass mode so the beam travels on.

components.name: 28-ID-D detectors
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.5 gives 36.5–39.5 m. The displayed position is the start of this range.
components.text: Scattered photons from the D sample are recorded by pixel-array detectors on the diffractometer arm or a long-distance positioner, 1 to 4 m from the sample. Farther away, each speckle spreads over more pixels, so finer speckle can be resolved.

components.name: Diamond single-crystal side-bounce monochromator for F, 28ID-MN-3
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.8 records path length along F from the straight-section centre. FDR Table 4.5 also lists the station position.
components.text: The second diamond crystal, 10 m farther along the shared beam, reflects 25 or 35 keV about 23° outboard into F. The rest of the radiation passes through. Two diamond reflections give nearly the same angle. The (022) reflection selects the undulator's 5th harmonic at 25 keV with a deflection 2θ = 22.68°, and the (004) reflection selects the 7th harmonic at 35 keV with 2θ = 22.91°. Switching energy therefore changes the deflection by only 0.23°.

components.name: Secondary collimator 28ID-SC-2, after second SCM
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.6 records path length from the straight-section centre.
components.text: A second shielding block confines stray radiation after the second diamond crystal. Its openings pass the continuing beams. It stops stray radiation travelling straight on from spreading further along the beamline.

components.name: Mono-beam slits 28ID-SL-9
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.8 records path length along F from the straight-section centre.
components.text: Adjustable jaws pass the central coherent part of the reflected 25 or 35 keV beam before F's first lens stack. A smaller opening raises the speckle contrast at the cost of flux.

components.name: Moveable mono beam stop 28ID-BS-3, end of D, manual
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.7 records path length along D/E from the straight-section centre.
components.text: A manual beam stop is installed at the end of hutch D. When it is in place, the 15 keV beam ends here, so people can safely work in hutch E while station D runs.

components.name: CRL unit 1 for F, 28ID-CR-7
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.8 records path length along F from the straight-section centre.
components.text: The first F focusing stage uses stacked beryllium compound refractive lenses inside the optics hutch, with a 50 µm tip radius. Up to 19 lenses are used for position F/1 and 12 for F/2; a second stack near each sample completes the zoom.

components.name: Beam visualization monitor 28ID-BD-4
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.8 records path length along F from the straight-section centre.
components.text: Staff locate the F beam during alignment using a fluorescent screen and camera. The monitor sits just after the branch's first lens stack, so staff can align the 25 or 35 keV beam after its crystal and lenses.

components.name: Silicon single-crystal side-bounce monochromator for G, 28ID-MN-4
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.9 records path length along G from the straight-section centre. FDR Table 4.5 also lists the station position.
components.text: The final monochromator reflects 75 or 105 keV X-rays from silicon about 5° inboard, toward the ring, into G. These high energies penetrate thick samples and vessels. Two silicon crystals provide the (022) and (004) reflections, which select the undulator's 15th and 21st harmonics of a 5 keV fundamental at almost the same deflection, 2θ ≈ 4.93–4.98°. The design range of this branch is 45–105 keV; 75 and 105 keV are the settings listed in 2026.

components.name: Monochromatic shutter 28ID-SH-3, P8-20
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.8 records path length along F from the straight-section centre.
components.text: The F shutter blocks the monochromatic, single-energy beam. Closing it makes hutch F safe to enter while the other three branches keep running.

components.name: Mono-beam slits 28ID-SL-8
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.7 records path length along D/E from the straight-section centre.
components.text: The 15 keV beam is trimmed just before station E's second lens stack. The opening sets the beam area and coherence reaching the laser-deposition chamber 1.8 m downstream.

components.name: CRL unit 2 for E, 28ID-CR-6
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.7 records path length along D/E from the straight-section centre.
components.text: The second E focusing stage is 1.5 m before the laser-deposition chamber, with up to 64 beryllium lenses of 50 µm tip radius. Together with the first stack in the optics hutch, the spot at E ranges between about 1.3 × 0.5 µm and 15 × 5.3 µm horizontally × vertically at 15 keV.

components.name: Mono-beam slits 28ID-SL-12
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.9 records path length along G from the straight-section centre.
components.text: The central part of the high-energy G beam passes through these jaws before the first lens stack. The slits sit 1.3 m after the silicon crystal that picks out G's energy.

components.name: Window 28ID-WN-4
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.7 records path length along D/E from the straight-section centre.
components.text: The E vacuum path ends at a thin diamond or beryllium window. Both are made of light atoms, so 15 keV X-rays pass through almost unhindered.

components.name: Shielded pipe through A, 28ID-ST-3
components.distanceNote: The position is not tabulated. The pipe is drawn approximately from SH-3 to the A outboard wall at about 42.5 m path length.
components.text: The F beam travels through a shielded pipe from the optics hutch's side wall into F. Bent about 23° outboard by its diamond crystal, the F branch leaves 28-ID-A roughly 42.5 m along its path.

components.name: CRL unit 1 for G, 28ID-CR-10, nickel lenses
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.9 records path length along G from the straight-section centre.
components.text: The first G focusing stage is upstream in the optics hutch. At 75 to 105 keV, refraction is weak in beryllium. The design specifies nickel lenses for stronger focusing, with up to 19 lenses for G/1 and 15 for G/2, each of 50 µm tip radius. Whether the nickel lenses were built as designed is not confirmed.

components.name: Beam visualization monitor 28ID-BD-5
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.9 records path length along G from the straight-section centre.
components.text: Staff locate the G beam during alignment using a fluorescent screen and camera. The monitor sits just after G's first lens stack, at 42.3 m along the G path.

components.name: Monochromatic shutter 28ID-SH-4, P8-20
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.9 records path length along G from the straight-section centre.
components.text: The G shutter blocks the monochromatic, single-energy beam. Closing it makes the long G hutch safe to enter while the other branches keep running; the tunable beam crosses G inside its own shielded pipe.

components.name: 28-ID-E pulsed-laser-deposition diffractometer, PLD, with HAXPES
components.distanceNote: The station position is tabulated in FDR Table 4.5.
components.text: In pulsed-laser deposition, or PLD, laser pulses vaporize material from a target. The material deposits on a substrate as an oxide film. X-ray diffraction measures the growing layers. Hard X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy, or HAXPES, measures emitted-electron energies to determine chemistry and electronic state. It uses 10 keV X-rays from a separate twisted monochromator. A published system of this kind, then at APS 33-ID-D, worked at 4–12 keV with a Scienta EW4000 analyser; that the same system moved to 28-ID-E is likely but not confirmed.

components.name: Shielded pipe through A, 28ID-ST-4
components.distanceNote: The position is approximate and not tabulated. The A downstream wall is about 43.4 m.
components.text: The G beam travels through a shielded pipe between the optics hutch and G. Between the two hutches it crosses a 2.6 m walk-through vestibule, together with the tunable branch's shielded pipe.

components.name: White-beam shielded transport 28ID-ST-1, 43.5–60.6 m
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.6 records path length from the straight centre. The displayed position is the start of the 43.5 to 60.6 m transport.
components.text: The tunable beam travels through a 17 m lead-shielded pipe from the optics hutch, across G and into B and C. This path is shielded from experiments in G. The pipe connects to shielded enclosure SE-1, containing the first focusing stage and shutter.

components.name: Mono-beam slits 28ID-SL-10
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.8 records path length along F from the straight-section centre.
components.text: The F beam is trimmed before F/1's second lens stack, 1.8 m ahead of the sample. The slit opening sets how much of the beam's coherent core reaches the diffractometer.

components.name: 28-ID-E detectors
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.5 gives 44.0–47.5 m. The displayed position is the start of this range.
components.text: Scattered X-rays from the growing film are recorded by area detectors behind the laser-deposition chamber. Detector positions range from about 1 to 4.5 m behind the sample.

components.name: CRL unit 2 for F position 1, 28ID-CR-8
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.8 records path length along F from the straight-section centre.
components.text: The second F/1 focusing stage is 1.5 m before the sample, with up to 63 beryllium lenses of 50 µm tip radius. With the first stack in the optics hutch, it sets the spot size at F/1 without moving the focus.

components.name: Window 28ID-WN-5
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.8 records path length along F from the straight-section centre.
components.text: The vacuum path ends at a thin diamond or beryllium window 1.2 m before F/1. Beyond it the beam reaches the sample environment.

components.name: 28-ID-F position 1: Huber hexapod diffractometer
components.distanceNote: The station position is tabulated in FDR Table 4.5.
components.text: Teams mount reaction cells and chambers on the Huber hexapod diffractometer at the front of F. When the rear position F/2 is in use, the diffractometer retracts in beam-pass mode so the beam reaches the growth reactor behind it. The directory lists a hexapod diffractometer and a growth chamber in F without saying which position hosts which; the model assumes the diffractometer is at F/1.

components.name: 28-ID-F/1 detectors
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.5 gives 46.5–48.5 m.
components.text: Speckle from F/1 is recorded by pixel-array detectors 1 to 3 m behind the sample. In beam-pass mode they move aside for beam transmission to F/2.

components.name: Mono-beam slits 28ID-SL-11
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.8 records path length along F from the straight-section centre.
components.text: The F beam is trimmed before F/2's second lens stack. The opening sets the coherent beam area reaching F/2, 1.8 m downstream.

components.name: Mono beam stop 28ID-BS-4, end of E
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.7 records path length along D/E from the straight-section centre.
components.text: The D/E beam ends at a stop behind station E. It absorbs the 15 keV beam after it has passed the laser-deposition chamber and its detectors.

components.name: CRL unit 2 for F position 2, 28ID-CR-9
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.8 records path length along F from the straight-section centre.
components.text: The second F/2 focusing stage is 1.5 m before the growth reactor, with up to 63 beryllium lenses of 50 µm tip radius. With the first stack in the optics hutch, it sets the spot size on the growing crystal without moving the focus.

components.name: Window 28ID-WN-6
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.8 records path length along F from the straight-section centre.
components.text: The vacuum path ends at a thin diamond or beryllium window before the growth reactor. The high-energy X-rays then pass through the reactor's quartz wall.

components.name: Photon mask 28ID-PM-1
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.6 records path length from the straight-section centre.
components.text: The photon mask is a metal aperture inside the shielded SE-1 enclosure. It absorbs any part of the tunable beam that strays from its intended path, protecting the lenses and pipes downstream.

components.name: Collimator 28ID-BC-2
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.6 records path length from the straight-section centre.
components.text: The tunable beam passes through an opening in a heavy collimator inside SE-1. The surrounding block absorbs stray radiation. It sits just behind the photon mask.

components.name: Mono-beam slits 28ID-SL-13
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.9 records path length along G from the straight-section centre.
components.text: The G beam is trimmed before G/1's second lens stack, 2.8 m ahead of the sample. The opening sets the beam area transmitted downstream.

components.name: 28-ID-F position 2, metal-organic chemical vapour deposition chamber, MOCVD
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.5 records the station position. Assigning MOCVD to F/2 is a model assumption.
components.text: Gallium nitride crystals grow from gases such as ammonia and triethylgallium in a heated quartz reactor. This metal-organic chemical vapour deposition, or MOCVD, process is used for LEDs and power-electronics chips. X-rays pass through the quartz wall for measurements of successive growth layers. Sample motion must stay well below a micrometre to preserve speckle stability. Its predecessor at APS 12-ID-D had a fused-quartz chamber 70 mm across with 2 mm walls, working from vacuum to 3.75 atmospheres above ambient. Placing it at F/2 is an assumption of the model.

specs.chamberWall: Fused quartz, 70 mm inside diameter × 2 mm wall thickness; predecessor instrument in Ju et al. 2017
specs.precursors: NH₃ and triethylgallium for GaN growth in Ju et al. 2019

components.name: CRL unit 2 for G position 1, 28ID-CR-11, nickel
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.9 records path length along G from the straight-section centre.
components.text: The second G/1 focusing stage is designed for up to 66 nickel lenses of 50 µm tip radius, 2.5 m before the sample. Nickel is chosen because it bends these very energetic X-rays more strongly than beryllium. The design flux at G/1 is 0.21–1.2 × 10¹¹ photons per second at 105 keV, calculated for the planned superconducting undulators.

components.name: Mono-beam conditioning slits 28ID-SL-3
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.6 records path length from the straight-section centre.
components.text: The tunable beam is trimmed before its first focusing stage inside SE-1. A smaller opening passes fewer coherent modes, increasing speckle contrast while reducing flux.

components.name: Window 28ID-WN-7
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.9 records path length along G from the straight-section centre.
components.text: The vacuum path ends at a thin diamond or beryllium window before G/1. Both low-atomic-number materials transmit 75 to 105 keV X-rays with little absorption.

components.name: Transfocator 1 for B and C, 28ID-CR-1
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.6 records path length from the straight-section centre.
components.text: The first B/C focusing stage uses a transfocator, a vacuum box containing 13 movable beryllium-lens stacks. Inserting or removing stacks changes the lens count and focusing strength remotely. Stacks contain 1 to 16 lenses with tip radii from 100 to 1,000 µm for fine focusing increments. Some lenses focus in one direction only. Up to 47 lenses are used for B and 35 for C. The lenses are inside shielded enclosure SE-1, allowing changes independently of the fixed-energy branches.

specs.2D lens stacks: R = 1,000, 500, 300, 200 and 100 µm, 1 lens each; R = 100 µm stacks with 2, 4, 8, 16 and 16 lenses
specs.1D lens stacks: R = 1,000, 500 and 500 µm, with 1, 1 and 2 lenses respectively
specs.motions: x, y, z, pitch and yaw under ultra-high vacuum

components.name: 28-ID-F/2 detectors
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.5 gives 50.5–53.5 m.
components.text: Speckle from F/2 is recorded by pixel-array detectors 1 to 4 m behind the growth reactor. From farther away each speckle covers more pixels, which helps resolve the fine speckle from a growing crystal surface.

components.name: Shutter 28ID-SH-1, P4-40
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.6 records path length from the straight-section centre.
components.text: The tunable branch has a P4-40 shutter inside SE-1. Teams at B and C can open and close their beam without affecting anyone else.

components.name: 28-ID-G position 1: Huber hexapod diffractometer
components.distanceNote: The station position is tabulated in FDR Table 4.5.
components.text: Samples and reaction vessels for 75 or 105 keV measurements are mounted on a shared Huber hexapod diffractometer in G. It serves surface, general and high-energy diffraction, and moves aside in beam-pass mode to feed the rear position G/2.

components.name: 28-ID-G/1 detectors
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.5 gives 53.0–55.0 m.
components.text: Scattered photons from G/1 are recorded by area detectors 1 to 3 m behind the sample. At 75–105 keV most X-rays would pass through a thin silicon sensor unrecorded, so these detectors need dense, heavy-element sensors; the models used are not published.

components.name: Mono-beam slits 28ID-SL-14
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.9 records path length along G from the straight-section centre.
components.text: The G beam is trimmed before G/2's second lens stack, 1.8 m ahead of the sample. The opening sets the beam area reaching the rear experiment.

components.name: Mono beam stop 28ID-BS-5, end of F
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.8 records path length along F from the straight-section centre.
components.text: The F beam ends at a stop behind the growth reactor and detectors. It absorbs whatever remains of the 25 or 35 keV beam.

components.name: CRL unit 2 for G position 2, 28ID-CR-12, nickel
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.9 records path length along G from the straight-section centre.
components.text: The second G/2 focusing stage is designed for up to 107 nickel lenses of 50 µm tip radius, 1.5 m before the sample. So many are needed because even nickel bends such energetic X-rays only slightly. In the design table, the spot at G/2 ranges from about 1.0 × 0.3 µm to 11 × 3.2 µm at 45 keV.

components.name: Window 28ID-WN-8
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.9 records path length along G from the straight-section centre.
components.text: The vacuum path ends at a thin diamond or beryllium window before G/2. Beyond it the beam travels the last 1.2 m to the sample.

components.name: 28-ID-G position 2, rear instrument position
components.distanceNote: The station position is tabulated in FDR Table 4.5.
components.text: G/2 is reserved for large, long-running instruments supplied by partner teams. The design report names bulk-crystal-growth systems and an environmental load frame as examples. It receives the beam when the front instrument moves aside, and which instrument occupies it in 2026 is not specified.

components.name: 28-ID-G/2 detectors
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.5 gives 57.0–60.0 m.
components.text: Scattered photons from G/2 are recorded by area detectors 1 to 4 m behind the sample, near the end of G. Like those at G/1, they need dense, heavy-element sensors to stop 75–105 keV X-rays; the models are not published.

components.name: Mono beam stop 28ID-BS-6, end of G
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.9 records path length along G from the straight-section centre.
components.text: The G beam ends at a stop 60.5 m from the source. It absorbs the very-high-energy beam that remains after the G/2 sample.

components.name: Beam visualization monitor 28ID-BD-2
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.6 records path length from the straight-section centre.
components.text: Staff locate the tunable beam at the entrance of B using a fluorescent screen and camera. X-ray fluorescence on the screen indicates the beam position.

components.name: Mono-beam conditioning slits 28ID-SL-4
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.6 records path length from the straight-section centre.
components.text: The tunable beam is trimmed before station B's second lens stack. The slits pass only the beam's most coherent central part, which keeps the speckle contrast high.

components.name: Transfocator 2 for B, 28ID-CR-2
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.6 records path length from the straight-section centre.
components.text: The second B focusing stage is 1.5 m before the sample. Its transfocator has 15 movable beryllium-lens stacks, holding up to 180 lenses of 50 µm tip radius. With the first stack 13 m upstream, the 15 keV horizontal × vertical spot ranges from about 9.8 × 3.4 µm to 0.9 × 0.3 µm at a fixed focal plane. Larger spots transmit more flux. One-dimensional lenses correct astigmatism, unequal focusing in the two directions, and the slight distortion that heat causes in the optics upstream. The design tables disagree slightly: the listed stacks add up to 191 lenses, against a stated maximum of 180.

specs.2D lens stacks: R = 1,000, 500, 200 and 100 µm, 1 lens each; R = 50 µm stacks with 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64 and 64 lenses
specs.1D lens stacks: R = 50 µm stacks with 1, 2 and 4 lenses for astigmatism and heat-bump correction
specs.table inconsistency: Table 4.11 stack counts total 191 lenses; Table 4.12 gives a maximum of 180.

components.name: Window 28ID-WN-1
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.6 records path length from the straight-section centre.
components.text: The vacuum path ends at a thin diamond or beryllium window 1.2 m before station B's sample. Both are made of light atoms, so the X-rays pass through almost unhindered.

components.name: 28-ID-B shared hexapod diffractometer
components.distanceNote: The station position is tabulated in FDR Table 4.5.
components.text: Samples and small reaction cells are mounted on a six-legged hexapod and rotation stage at B. Scattered photons are recorded by detectors on an arm 1 to 2 m away or a separate positioner up to 4 m away. In the design, the tunable beam reaches it in spots from about 0.9 × 0.3 µm to 9.8 × 3.4 µm at 15 keV. The design flux, calculated for the planned superconducting undulators, is 6.8–37 × 10¹² photons per second at 15 keV and 4.2–11 × 10¹² at 60 keV; flux with today's interim undulators is not published.

components.name: 28-ID-B pixel-array detectors, arm and LDDP
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.5 gives detector range 65.5–68.5 m; value is the start of the range.
components.text: Speckle is recorded by pixel-array detectors on the diffractometer arm at 1 to 2 m for alignment, or on the long-distance positioner at 2 to 4 m for imaging. At those distances each speckle spreads over several pixels. The models are not published; the preliminary design envisioned photon-counting detectors with cadmium-telluride sensors and pixels of about 55 µm.

specs.sampleDetectorDistance_m: 1–2 on the arm; 2–4 on the LDDP

components.name: Moveable white-beam stop 28ID-BS-1, end of B
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.6 records path length from the straight-section centre.
components.text: A motorized stop at the end of B is rated to absorb the full white beam. When it is closed, the beam ends here, so people can safely build or adjust a large growth chamber in hutch C while station B runs.

components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.6 records path length from the straight-section centre.

instruments.name: Shared CHEX endstation, hexapod diffractometer and LDDP
instruments.text: The shared design for B, D, F and G has a hexapod mounted on a large rotation stage beside a vertical detector tower. The hexapod is a six-legged platform for precise translations and tilts. The preliminary design specified reaction chambers up to 50 kg, with stability better than one micrometre and one microradian. An alignment detector is placed on the diffractometer arm 1–2 m from the sample. For imaging and speckle measurements, the detector is placed 2–4 m away on a separate long-distance positioner, supported by air pads over a granite base. A third configuration places a zone-plate objective on the arm for interface microscopy. In beam-pass mode, all axes clear the beam pipe for a rear experiment. The 2026 directory lists general-purpose Huber hexapod diffractometers in D, F and G, but does not identify the manufacturer at B.
detectors: Pixel-array detectors; models are not published.
Scintillator-coupled CCD module in the FDR design.
sampleEnvironments: Compact CVD, ALD, sputtering and etching chambers in the preliminary design.

instruments.name: Oxide MBE chamber
instruments.text: At 28-ID-C, oxide molecular-beam epitaxy forms crystal layers in an ultra-high-vacuum chamber from beams of evaporated atoms, with ozone or oxygen supplied to form the oxide. The chamber angle is set on a goniometer, a precision rotation stage. X-ray diffraction through windows measures the layers during growth. On the tunable branch, measurements at an element's absorption edge distinguish the metal ions. This is inferred to be the oxide-growth system formerly at APS 33-ID-E, where Lee and colleagues measured layer rearrangement in 2014. The relocation is not explicitly documented.
sampleEnvironments: Oxide MBE in ultra-high vacuum with ozone or oxygen.

instruments.name: PLD diffractometer with HAXPES
instruments.text: In pulsed laser deposition, each laser pulse vaporizes target material in an oxygen background. The material deposits on a substrate to form an oxide film. Surface X-ray diffraction measures the atomic layers during growth. Hard X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy, or HAXPES, identifies chemistry and electronic states from the energies of emitted electrons. A separate "twisted" monochromator supplies 10 keV X-rays. A published predecessor at 33-ID-D combined these measurements with HAXPES at 4–12 keV and a Scienta EW4000 analyser.
sampleEnvironments: Pulsed laser deposition in an oxygen background.

instruments.name: MOCVD growth chamber on hexapod diffractometer
instruments.text: Semiconductor crystals such as gallium nitride form in a heated quartz reactor supplied with ammonia and metal-organic gases. This process is metal-organic chemical vapour deposition, or MOCVD. The 2026 directory lists the chamber in F with a Huber hexapod diffractometer. In the 12-ID-D predecessor, the sample was held still to much less than the beam size and the detector to about 25 µm at more than 1 m. Its Huber diffractometer was combined with a hexapod and separate near and far detector positioners. The fused-quartz reactor was 70 mm across with 2 mm walls, operating from vacuum to 3.75 atmospheres above ambient.
detectors: Photon-counting pixel-array detectors. The predecessor used a 512 × 512 GaAs LynX 1800 with 55 µm pixels.
sampleEnvironments: MOCVD with NH₃ and triethylgallium. The GaN benchmark in Ju et al. 2019 used growth near 800 K and annealing at 1,120 K.

instruments.name: High-energy hexapod diffractometer
instruments.text: At 28-ID-G, surface, general and high-energy diffraction measurements use a shared Huber hexapod diffractometer with 75 or 105 keV X-rays. These energies penetrate thick samples, furnaces and reaction vessels. Position G/2 behind it is reserved for large partner instruments, including the bulk-crystal-growth systems and environmental load frame proposed in the design report. Dense, heavy-element detector sensors are required for efficient absorption at these energies.
sampleEnvironments: Furnaces, load frames and bulk-growth systems in the proposed design.

geometryNotes:
The outboard beam from the upstream undulator runs straight through 28-ID-A, about 23.6 to 43.4 m, and a shielded transport through the outboard side of G at 43.5 to 60.6 m. Mini-enclosure SE-1 is at 48.2 to 52.2 m. The beam then enters B at about 60.7 to 69.5 m and C at about 69.7 to 78.6 m. FDR Fig. 4.2 and the MEDSI 2025 as-built ray trace support this arrangement.

The downstream undulator beam is angled 1 mrad inboard. Separation is approximately 1 mrad × distance, about 28 mm at 28 m and 40 mm at 40 m. Inside A, side-reflecting crystals split off D/E at 28.3 m, F at 38.3 m and G at 40.2 m. D/E and F turn about 23.2° outboard, away from the ring, crossing the tunable beam near their crystals. They leave A at path lengths about 33.4 m and 42.5 m respectively, scaled from FDR Fig. 4.2. G turns about 5° inboard toward the ring.

Distances are measured along each branch from the straight-section centre. The actual sources are at about ±1.23 m.

The model branch origins and angles are D/E at 28.3 m and +23.2°, F at 38.3 m and +23.0°, and G at 40.2 m and −5.0°. Positive angles are outboard.

D, E and F are rotated about 23° from the main axis. D/E are tandem hutches, while F and G each contain two instrument positions. Front instruments retract in beam-pass mode for rear-position measurements. Each station has CRL2, slits and a window about 1.2 to 2.8 m before the sample. Beamline vacuum ends at the window.

Horizontal reflection in the tunable fixed-exit DCM displaces the monochromatic beam sideways. A low-resolution 2025 ray-trace note indicates a photon-mask shift of 4 to 8 mm outboard for monochromatic operation. Beam height is about 1.4 m.

CHEX occupies floor space normally assigned to 28-BM and 29-BM, which have no beamlines, and to the short neighbouring 27-ID. Control Rooms D, E and F and the Sample Prep Lab are outboard of D/E/F. Control Room B is outboard; G and C control rooms are inboard. These positions follow FDR Fig. 4.2. The PDR specifies chemical exhaust and gas cabinets for B through G.

Station letters changed after the 2017 PDR. It used B/C, D and E for fixed branches and F/G for tunable branches. This exhibit uses FDR and as-built names.

Sector 28 was unoccupied in 2017 and later hosted the IDEA optics-test beamline until the 2023 shutdown. The canted front end and first optics enclosure 28-ID-A were built in 2018 and 2019.

In MEDSI 2025 Fig. 2, A, B and C boundaries agree with the FDR plan within about 0.2 m. G is shorter and narrower than the 2019 drawing. Its upstream wall is about 47.5 m rather than 44.9 m, and its outboard wall is about 0.45 m from the tunable axis beside ST-1. The inboard wall is about 1.9 to 2.7 m inboard. A double-door vestibule about 2.6 m long separates A and G.

interactiveIdeas.title: Harmonic selection for simultaneous experiments
interactiveIdeas.concept: An undulator-gap slider changes the fundamental E1 from 2–8 keV and displays harmonics at n·E1. Three crystals are placed at fixed angles, with diamond at 2θ = 23.2° and silicon at 2θ = 5.0°. Selecting a crystal changes its reflection among 111, 220 and 400. Branch illumination occurs when a harmonic matches the Bragg energy. Near E1 = 5 keV, the fixed-energy branches receive 15, 25/35 and 75/105 keV simultaneously. Unreflected light passes through the thin diamonds to the next crystal.
interactiveIdeas.whatUserLearns: Different harmonics are separated by crystal diffraction, allowing simultaneous fixed-energy experiments from one undulator beam.
interactiveIdeas.physicsToGetRight: Photon energy and wavelength are related by E[keV] = 12.398/λ[Å]. Bragg diffraction follows λ = 2d sinθ, with d = a/√(h²+k²+l²), a(C) = 3.5668 Å and a(Si) = 5.4310 Å. Undulator harmonics follow E_n = n·E1, where E1[keV] = 0.9496·E_e²[GeV]/(λu[cm](1+K²/2)). PDR Tables 6.10/6.13 give C(111) at 15 keV, 2θ = 23.15°; C(220) at 25 keV, 22.68°; C(400) at 35 keV, 22.91°; Si(220) at 75 keV, 4.93°; and Si(400) at 105 keV, 4.98°. The diamond reflections match the 3:5:7 harmonic ratios only approximately, with a ±0.5° angular mismatch. Forbidden silicon and diamond reflections such as 200 have no intensity. Even harmonics are weak on axis. Finite energy spread broadens high harmonics at n = 15–21.

interactiveIdeas.title: Focal spot and speckle resolution
interactiveIdeas.concept: Controls adjust X-ray energy, focal spot size and detector distance. Simulated speckle is displayed on a 55 µm pixel grid. As the spot grows, speckles become smaller than a pixel and measured contrast β falls.
interactiveIdeas.whatUserLearns: Resolving speckle requires a suitable combination of focal spot, detector distance and pixel size. At higher energy, the shorter wavelength reduces speckle size.
interactiveIdeas.physicsToGetRight: Speckle angular size is approximately λ/a. Resolution requires λR/a ≳ p. For p = 55 µm, the PDR gives a_max = 0.886λR/p ≈20·R[m]/E[keV] µm. At 35 keV and R = 4 m, a ≤2.3 µm. Coherent diffraction imaging requires oversampling ≥2. In the Gaussian Schell convention, coherence length ξ ≈λz/(2πσ); other conventions differ by π. At fixed brightness, coherent flux ∝B·λ² ∝E⁻².

interactiveIdeas.title: Layer growth and two-time correlations
interactiveIdeas.concept: An animated surface displays deposition, island nucleation, growth and coalescence. Plots display one anti-Bragg crystal-truncation-rod intensity oscillation per monolayer, diffuse speckle and a two-time correlation map. A control compares independent island nucleation with persistent island arrangements between layers, following Ju et al. 2019.
interactiveIdeas.whatUserLearns: Anti-Bragg intensity varies with atomic-layer coverage. Diffuse-speckle correlations measure how island arrangements persist between successive layers.
interactiveIdeas.physicsToGetRight: For fractional top-layer coverage θ, the kinematic anti-Bragg intensity is I ∝|1 − 2θ|², with a period of one monolayer. Diffuse island scattering oscillates out of phase with the crystal-truncation rod and peaks at half-integer monolayer coverage. Ju et al. 2019 define C(t1,t2) = <ΔI(Q,t1)ΔI(Q,t2)> / <Ī(Q,t1)Ī(Q,t2)>, where ΔI = I − Ī and Ī is the pixel-smoothed mean. The diagonal is the speckle contrast. Positive, zero and negative C indicate correlated, uncorrelated and anti-correlated island arrangements. Persistent arrangements produce off-diagonal correlations with a one-monolayer period. The GaN benchmark growth rate was about 1.25 × 10⁻³ ML/s, with 10 s frames.

interactiveIdeas.title: Two-stack refractive zoom focusing
interactiveIdeas.concept: Two transfocator stacks are displayed, with CRL1 far upstream and CRL2 1.5 m before the sample. Lens selections change the sample spot from about 10 µm to below 1 µm while keeping the focal plane fixed. A second view displays the different focal distances of harmonics and their rejection by a slit near the focus.
interactiveIdeas.whatUserLearns: X-ray refraction is weak, so many lenses are needed at high energy. Lens material, count and spacing determine focus and transmission. The G design uses nickel rather than beryllium.
interactiveIdeas.physicsToGetRight: For N biconcave parabolic lenses of apex radius R, the thin-lens focal length is f = R/(2Nδ). The refractive decrement is δ ≈r_e λ² n_e/2π. For Be, δ ≈1.5 × 10⁻⁶ at 15 keV and 2.8 × 10⁻⁷ at 35 keV, with δ ∝E⁻². Magnification in two-stack source imaging depends on both stacks. Absorption limits aperture and lowers transmission as N rises. The PDR predicts harmonic rejection up to about 10⁵ with chromatic focusing and slits. FDR maximum counts are 180 Be lenses for B and 107 Ni lenses for G/2. FDR Fig. 4.4 predicts that adding upstream CRL1 lenses increases the station-B horizontal focal spot from about 0.9 to 8 µm at 35 keV. Transmission rises from about 0.2 to 0.64 at 35 keV and to 0.84 at 15 keV. The smallest spots therefore have lower flux.

interactiveIdeas.title: Emittance and coherent fraction
interactiveIdeas.concept: Phase-space ellipses display the size and divergence of the pre-upgrade and upgraded electron beams beside the diffraction-limited ellipse λ/4π. An energy slider from 5–100 keV changes the calculated coherent fraction and coherent flux.
interactiveIdeas.whatUserLearns: Emittance combines beam size and divergence. A 70× reduction increases coherent fraction, particularly at high energy. The diffraction limit depends on wavelength.
interactiveIdeas.physicsToGetRight: Per plane, coherent fraction ≈(λ/4π)/(Σ·Σ'), where Σ = √(σe² + σr²), Σ' = √(σe'² + σr'²), σr = √(2λL)/4π and σr' = √(λ/2L). APS-U flat-beam inputs are σx = 14.5 µm, σx' = 2.75 µrad, σy = 3.08 µm and σy' = 1.29 µrad. Pre-upgrade inputs are σx = 280 µm, σx' = 11.6 µrad, σy = 10 µm and σy' = 3.4 µrad. At 25 keV, the result is about 2% for APS-U and 0.01% before the upgrade. This is an idealized estimate. Energy spread at σδ ≈0.14% further reduces high-harmonic brightness.

interactiveIdeas.title: Coherent transmission through a reactor
interactiveIdeas.concept: A cutaway MOCVD reactor has 2 mm fused-quartz walls. An energy control changes plots of transmitted total flux and coherent flux, showing their different optimum energies.
interactiveIdeas.whatUserLearns: Higher-energy X-rays penetrate reactor walls more effectively, but coherent source flux falls with energy. Their combination determines the optimum energy for a coherent experiment.
interactiveIdeas.physicsToGetRight: Transmission is T = exp(−μt), with a 4 mm total quartz path through two walls. Attenuation μ(E) is from NIST XCOM or xraylib. Multiplying transmission by source coherent flux, proportional to B·λ², gives the coherent flux at the sample. Ju et al. 2017, Fig. 2 compares the then-current 12-ID-D undulator, 3.0 cm × 2.0 m, with projected APS-U sources. The optimum energies through 4 mm of quartz are about 30 keV for total flux and 23 keV for coherent flux.

funFacts: Three fixed-energy experiments share one undulator beam. Two thin diamond crystals reflect different harmonics at 15 keV and 25 or 35 keV. The remaining light passes through to a silicon crystal, where 75 or 105 keV is reflected into the final branch. This arrangement is described in the PDR and APS Beamline Directory.

The D/E and F beams are deflected about 23° sideways by diamond crystals. This is much larger than typical synchrotron-mirror deflections of a few milliradians, such as 4 mrad at 25-ID. These values are from the PDR, Beamline Directory and FDR.
At 75–105 keV, refraction in beryllium is weak. The G-station design therefore specifies nickel lenses in FDR Table 4.12.

For the GaN growth measurements in Ju et al. 2019, the monochromator was removed to obtain enough coherent X-rays. The resulting pink beam included the undulator harmonic peak, about 1% wide in energy.
An APS-U-design canted front end was installed at 28-ID and tested with beam on the old ring in November 2018. This FDR milestone preceded the upgrade dark period by more than four years.
Sector 28 was empty in 2017. Before CHEX construction, the temporary IDEA beamline was used there to test optics for preserving APS-U coherence. The history is recorded in the PDR and APS News 2022.

As of September 2026, the installed sources are interim permanent-magnet undulators. The APS ID table and Strategic Plan 2025–29 describe planned replacement with superconducting undulators operated at 4.2 K.

B/C and D/E each have tandem hutch pairs. A beam stop in the front hutch permits assembly and adjustment of growth chambers in the rear hutch during a front-hutch experiment. F and G each have two positions in one long hutch. In their beam-pass configuration, the front instrument is moved aside for the rear experiment. These arrangements are described in the FDR and PDR.
The PDR predicted about 1 terabyte of data per day from each of four simultaneous experiments.
APS News reported 45 pm·rad measured emittance at 50 mA in 2024, below the previous record of 134 pm·rad.

Community workshops preceded CHEX construction. A MEDSI 2018 project listing named Robert Winarski and Brian Stephenson as science leads. The APS feature page and XSD-SSM group page list Matt Highland, Zhan Zhang, Hua Zhou, Hawoong Hong and Tomoya Kawaguchi on the beamline team within the APS Surface Scattering and Microdiffraction group.
The APS Strategic Plan 2025–29 predicts about three times higher brightness from superconducting undulators than from the interim permanent-magnet devices above 50 keV.

openQuestions: The interim source-to-branch mapping is inferred rather than stated explicitly for 28-ID. The upstream 2.8 cm source is assigned to the outboard tunable path and the downstream 3.0 cm source to the inboard fixed-energy path, following the canting convention in the FDR 6-ID and 34-ID descriptions and the FDR power tables. The directory lists "SCU0" for B/C, conflicting with the September 2026 ID table.

The 18.5 mm superconducting-undulator pair has no confirmed installation date. The Strategic Plan gives 2026–2027; the 22 September 2026 ID table still lists HPMUs. FDR Chapter 4 gives 1.3 m length, while Chapter 3 gives 1.2 m magnetic length.

The tunable-branch ranges differ between sources. The FDR text gives 5–60 keV; MEDSI 2025 and the PDR give 15–60 keV; the directory gives 6–30 keV with Si(111) and the interim source. The feature page gives 5–104 keV for the entire sector.
MEDSI 2025 gives 15–60 keV for the selectable-energy branches. The directory lists 75 and 105 keV for G, while the FDR design range is 45–105 keV.

The feature page gives an upper sector limit of 104 keV, while the directory gives 105 keV for G with Si(004). This may be rounding or the 103.9 keV value in PDR Table 6.13 for Si(400) on the 15th harmonic of a 6.93 keV fundamental. The reason is not documented.
Installation of the Si(311) DCM crystal pair and optional double-multilayer monochromator is unconfirmed. The design allows "DCM or DMM".
The design and position of the "twisted monochromator" for 10 keV HAXPES at 28-ID-E are unpublished.

The installed single-crystal monochromator details are unconfirmed, including diamond thickness, Bragg or Laue geometry, cooling, D/E use of (022)/(004) crystals, and the graphite-filter position. The FDR specifies LN₂ cooling, while the PDR emphasizes symmetric Bragg geometry.
The installed transfocator models and lens inventories are unconfirmed. FDR Tables 4.11–4.12 give design values, including nickel lenses for G.
The pixel-array detector models, sensor materials and pixel sizes are unpublished. Construction of the long-distance detector positioners as shown in FDR Fig. 4.8 is unconfirmed.
The assignment of the MOCVD chamber and hexapod diffractometer to F positions is unconfirmed, as is the instrument at G/2.
The C oxide-MBE, E PLD/HAXPES and F MOCVD systems are strongly suggested to be relocated instruments from 33-ID-E, 33-ID-D and 12-ID-D, respectively. Relocation is not stated explicitly.

Hutch wall positions, widths and heights in the exhibit are scaled from FDR Fig. 4.2 and the 2025 ray-trace plan. Exact dimensions and front-end tunnel component positions are unavailable; only the exit mask and collimator positions are tabulated.
FDR Section 4-2.3 specifies a 2 × 1 mm exit aperture for CHEX. FDR Table 4.6 and Chapter 3 give the standard CUFE aperture as 2 × 2 mm. The installed aperture is unconfirmed.
Measured flux and focal sizes with the interim HPMUs are unpublished. FDR Table 4.10 assumes superconducting sources.
The directory status "Not Currently Operational" for B/C appears stale relative to stage 5 on the 5 October 2026 commissioning chart.
User access to pink or white beam in B/C is unconfirmed. White-beam stops are present, and the PDR lists pink beam as an option.
FDR Table 4.11 lists CRL-2 stacks for B that sum to 191 two-dimensional 50 µm lenses. Table 4.12 gives a maximum of 180. The installed count is unknown.
The August 2025 update projected general-user entry in run 2026-1 or 2026-2. As of 5 October 2026, no CHEX station had reached stage 6, and no new start date had been published.
